claims.claim: Spain's legal foundation: drug consumption and possession for personal use have never been criminalized, a position rooted in the constitutional protection of privacy and personal autonomy (Constitution of 1978), and the Supreme Court's 'shared consumption' (consumo compartido) case-law tradition holds that non-commercial consumption among a closed group is not inherently criminal — this doctrine is the legal seed of the cannabis club model.
claims.source: ICEERS, 'Spain' legal information page (drug law overview)
claims.quote: Drug consumption and possession for personal use are not criminalized in Spain
claims.note: The same page names 'the Supreme Court doctrine of shared consumption' as the basis for consumer associations, and flags that the doctrine was later revised against large clubs (see the 2015 Supreme Court claim). Spain also relied on Art. 3(2) of the 1988 UN Convention, which lets states decline to criminalize personal consumption where it conflicts with their constitution.

claims.claim: The honest counterweight: Organic Law 4/2015 on the Protection of Citizen Security (the 'Ley Mordaza' / gag law, in force 1 July 2015) made consumption or possession of drugs in public places a serious ADMINISTRATIVE infraction, fined in the 601–30,000 euro band (art. 36.16) — no criminal record, but a real and heavily used penalty. Private use remains outside both criminal and administrative sanction.
claims.source: Ley Orgánica 4/2015, de 30 de marzo, de protección de la seguridad ciudadana (BOE); fine range corroborated by Cannabis Europa legal analysis
claims.note: The nickname 'Ley Mordaza' and civil-liberties criticism are documented in European Parliament question E-8-2015-006729 (europarl.europa.eu). Corroborating fine-range analysis: https://cannabis-europa.com/insights/is-cannabis-legal-in-spain/ (most fines land at the 601-euro floor).

claims.claim: Basque origin of the cannabis social club: the Kalamudia association staged the first large public protest plantation in the Basque Country in 1997, repeated it without prosecution, and dissolved around 2001–2002 into smaller local associations cultivating for their own members — the template that became the CSC model. Pannagh was founded in Bilbao on 22 February 2003 and entered the Basque General Register of Associations on 20 June 2003; its president Martín Barriuso (ex-Kalamudia, later head of the FAC federation) was arrested with two members while harvesting for the club in 2005, and the favorable Basque court outcome in 2006 is credited with precipitating the nationwide CSC expansion.
claims.source: Pannagh, 'Pannagh: history, trials and legacy of a pioneering cannabis social club in Spain'; ENCOD profile 'Pannagh, Spain'
claims.note: ENCOD corroboration: https://encod.org/en/cannabis-social-club/examples-of-cscs-in-europe/pannagh-spain/. The literature also records the Cannabis Tasters Club of Barcelona (CCCB), 2001, as the first club defined as a 'cannabis social club' as such. Pannagh's own site is the association's account of itself — primary but partisan.

claims.claim: The member-association legal theory, as codified by its international students: Transform Drug Policy Foundation's Spain briefing defines the model — non-profit, closed-membership, collective cultivation, no profit motive to recruit new users — dates the first CSC to 2001, counts roughly 400 clubs, and argues the Spanish experience proves 'legalisation without commercialisation' is possible, which is why the model is studied worldwide (Uruguay and Malta later wrote CSCs into statute).
claims.source: Transform Drug Policy Foundation, 'Cannabis social clubs in Spain: legalisation without commercialisation' (blog + 2018 briefing PDF)
claims.quote: Cannabis social clubs (CSCs) are private, non-profit organisations in which cannabis is collectively grown and distributed to registered members.
claims.note: Further verbatim from the same source: 'The first CSC was founded in 2001'; 'There are thought to be roughly 400 CSCs or similar associations in Spain'; 'The growth of the CSC model in Spain demonstrates that cannabis legalisation does not have to mean commercialisation.' Briefing PDF: https://transformdrugs.org/assets/files/PDFs/cannabis-in-spain-briefing-2018.pdf

claims.claim: The Barcelona boom, in numbers: Catalonia went from about 40 cannabis clubs in 2011 to more than 500 with over 165,000 members by 2014, at which point Barcelona city hall ordered the closure of a third of the city's 145 clubs and began zoning them — the press dubbed the city 'the Amsterdam of southern Europe'.
claims.quote: In 2011, just 40 such cannabis clubs existed in Catalonia. By 2014, according to Tio, that number had jumped to more than 500 with over 165,000 members
claims.note: The 145-club closure order is reported via Bloomberg, 'Barcelona Is Fighting an Overdose of Cannabis Clubs' (2014-06-13, https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2014-06-13/barcelona-is-fighting-an-overdose-of-cannabis-clubs). Figures attributed to club-federation spokesman Eric Asensio/'Tio' in the Reason piece; counts vary by source (400–500 range for 2014).

claims.claim: The arc bends back — regional regulation struck down: Navarra's 2014 foral law regulating cannabis-user associations (Spain's first) was challenged by the central government and annulled by the Constitutional Court in 2017; Catalonia's Law 13/2017 (passed by popular legislative initiative, with registration, health standards and operating limits) was annulled in full by ruling STC 100/2018 of 19 September 2018, the Court holding unanimously that narcotics regulation is exclusive state competence under criminal law.
claims.source: Ara (English edition), 'Spain's Constitutional Court overturns Catalan law on cannabis clubs'; academic corroboration in International Journal of Drug Policy
claims.quote: marijuana's regulation must be in the hands of the State, which has sole responsibility for establishing the criminal penalties for narcotics
claims.note: Academic arc: 'Contentious legality in decentralized governance: The rise and decline of cannabis social clubs in Spain', https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955395926000575. TNI analysis: https://www.tni.org/en/article/the-new-decisions-of-the-constitutional-court-the-end-of-cannabis-tolerance-in-spain. The Navarra annulment is widely cited as STC 144/2017.

claims.claim: The Supreme Court's 2015 revision of shared consumption: in the case line arising from the Bilbao association Ebers, the Court held that organized cultivation and distribution of cannabis by a club of 290 members constitutes a drug-trafficking offense — drawing the criminal ceiling over large, open-membership clubs while leaving the small closed-circle doctrine intact.
claims.source: Poder Judicial (Spanish judiciary) news release, via ICEERS Spain page
claims.quote: El Supremo considera delito el cultivo y distribucion organizada de cannabis por un club de 290 socios
claims.note: Quote is the judiciary's own headline (verbatim as linked from the ICEERS page, diacritics normalized in URL form). The judgment is commonly cited in the literature as STS 484/2015 (the 'Ebers' case); ICEERS describes the shared-consumption doctrine as 'recently revised' by this line of rulings.

claims.claim: Hemp, the kingdom's strategic fiber: from 1665 to 1808 the Spanish crown ran a sustained military supply system for canamo — hemp made the match-cord, rigging and sails of the fleet — and royal policy tried to extend hemp harvests to the American possessions specifically to escape dependence on Russian hemp bought in the Baltic; entrepreneurs became middlemen for the Russian purchases when that failed.
claims.source: Manuel Diaz-Ordonez, 'El abastecimiento militar de canamo para el imperio espanol (1665-1808): globalizacion, estado y empresarios en el largo Siglo XVIII', Espacio Tiempo y Forma, Serie IV Historia Moderna (UNED), 2019, doi:10.5944/etfiv.32.2019.22239
claims.quote: con el se producia cuerda mecha, y jarcia y velas para el aparejo de los veleros
claims.note: Quote from the article abstract (Spanish; accents present in original). Same abstract: hemp became 'un producto globalizado por las necesidades estrategicas de los imperios'. Related English-language scholarship: 'Cannabis Yarn in the Spanish and English Empires' (War & Society 40:1, doi:10.1080/07292473.2021.1860317).

claims.claim: Callosa de Segura (Alicante) is Spain's living monument to working hemp: the town calls itself the 'capital del canamo', was the country's leading manufacturer of hemp rope, nets and espadrille soles until synthetic fibers displaced the craft in the 1960s, and its Museo del Canamo — founded 1986 in the 1920 municipal slaughterhouse and recognized as an official Museographic Collection on 24 March 1994 — exhibits the complete cycle from seed to spun thread, rope-braiding, net-making and footwear.
claims.source: Ayuntamiento de Callosa de Segura, 'Museo del Canamo'; Wikipedia (es), 'Museo del Canamo "Roque Francisco Albert Lucas"'; Comunitat Valenciana tourism listing
claims.quote: Callosa se muestra especialmente orgullosa de sus origenes como capital del canamo.
claims.note: Quote from the town hall's museum page (Spanish, accents in original). Recognition date and founding year per https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_del_C%C3%A1%C3%B1amo_%22Roque_Francisco_Albert_Lucas%22 and https://www.comunitatvalenciana.com/en/alacant-alicante/callosa-de-segura/museums/cm-museo-etnologico-municipal-del-canamo-y-huerta. The museum stages live demonstrations of the old fiber-working methods.

claims.claim: Callosa's deep-time telling: hemp-industry popular histories date the town's hemp working to around 1300 and call medieval Callosa the largest producer of hemp-made goods — a claim carried by local pride and trade lore rather than by accessible scholarly documentation.
claims.source: Hempshopper 'Hemp History' series (industry telling); local tradition as relayed by the town's own 'capital del canamo' identity
claims.note: Named tellers: hempshopper.com (hemp trade site) and Callosa civic tradition. The documented record (museum, industrial peak, 1960s decline) is solid; the specific 1300 date and 'largest producer' superlative are the traditional telling and should be labeled as such on the wall.

claims.claim: Modern lawful industrial hemp, the legal facts: under the EU Common Agricultural Policy (Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, applying from 1 January 2023) hemp qualifies for support only if the variety's THC content is below 0.3% (raised from 0.2%), farmers must sow certified seed of varieties in the EU common catalogue, and the EU area under fibre hemp grew from 20,540 ha (2015) to 33,020 ha (2022). Spain cultivates industrial hemp inside this framework, though the Commission names France (over 60%), Germany (17%) and the Netherlands (5%) as the leading producers.
claims.source: European Commission, DG Agriculture and Rural Development, 'Hemp' crop page
claims.quote: Farmers must use certified seed of varieties listed in the EU common catalogue of varieties of agricultural plant species.
claims.note: Also verbatim from the same page: 'The variety of hemp being cultivated must have a THC content below 0.3%.' and 'Hemp is a crop grown across Europe... from 20,540 hectares (ha) in 2015 to 33,020 ha in 2022 (a 60% increase).' Honesty note: the EC page does not list Spain among the top growers; Spain's participation is a legal fact (CMS Spain cannabis guide, https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-a-legal-roadmap-to-cannabis/spain), not a market-leadership claim.

claims.claim: Ibiza inside the model: the island's scene runs on the same national member-association theory — and it is municipally documented, not just promoted. Ibiza's city council has issued opening licenses to 17 cannabis associations since 2018, and in March 2024 voted to regulate new openings through a municipal ordinance, suspending licenses for new associations in the meantime; in November 2023 members of the island's Domus Club protested outside the Ibiza courts over a police raid they said was carried out without a judicial order.
claims.source: Periodico de Ibiza, 'El Ayuntamiento de Ibiza regulara la apertura de nuevos clubes de cannabis en la ciudad'
claims.quote: el Consistorio ha dado licencia de apertura a 17 de estos establecimientos desde 2018
claims.note: The article describes the clubs in the standard national terms: they 'se abastecen y distribuyen la marihuana entre sus propios socios en un ambito privado' as 'circulos cerrados en los que no se alcanza a terceras personas' (verbatim, accents in original). Domus Club raid coverage: Canamo magazine, https://canamo.net/noticias/espana/un-club-de-cannabis-de-ibiza-denuncia-un-registro-de-la-policia-sin-orden-judicial

verify.wing: Spain — Cannabis Social Club Law & History

verdicts.claim: Spain's legal foundation: consumption/possession for personal use never criminalized, rooted in the 1978 Constitution's privacy/autonomy protection; Supreme Court 'consumo compartido' doctrine holds closed-group non-commercial consumption not inherently criminal and is the legal seed of the club model (ICEERS Spain page).
verdicts.evidence: ICEERS page says verbatim: "Drug consumption and possession for personal use are not criminalized in Spain and carry an administrative penalty only when performed in a public place" and cites "the Supreme Court doctrine of shared consumption (recently revised)" as what led to private consumer associations. The page nowhere mentions the Constitution of 1978, privacy, or personal autonomy; its 'recently revised' link is to the Supreme Court ruling that organized cultivation/distribution by a 290-member club IS a crime.
verdicts.correction: Keep the non-criminalization fact and the shared-consumption doctrine as the club model's seed, but drop the constitutional privacy/autonomy attribution — it is not in this source ('never been criminalized' is also stronger than the source's present-tense statement). Add that the source itself flags the doctrine as 'recently revised': the Supreme Court (2015) held that organized club-scale cultivation and distribution is criminal, so 'not inherently criminal' cannot be stated unqualified.

verdicts.claim: Organic Law 4/2015 (in force 1 July 2015) made public drug consumption/possession a serious administrative infraction under art. 36.16, fined 601–30,000 euros; no criminal record; private use outside both criminal and administrative sanction.
verdicts.evidence: BOE consolidated text: header "Entrada en vigor: 01/07/2015"; art. 36.16 (under infracciones graves): "El consumo o la tenencia ilícitos de drogas tóxicas, estupefacientes o sustancias psicotrópicas, aunque no estuvieran destinadas al tráfico, en lugares, vías, establecimientos públicos o transportes colectivos..."; art. 39.1: "las graves, con multa de 601 a 30.000 euros". The infraction is confined to public places, consistent with private use carrying no administrative sanction; ICEERS corroborates ("administrative penalty only when performed in a public place").

verdicts.claim: Basque origin: Kalamudia's 1997 public protest plantation, repeated without prosecution, dissolved ~2001–2002 into member-cultivating associations; Pannagh founded Bilbao 22 Feb 2003, registered 20 June 2003; president Martín Barriuso (ex-Kalamudia, FAC head) arrested with two members while harvesting in 2005; favorable 2006 Basque court outcome credited with precipitating nationwide CSC expansion.
verdicts.evidence: pannagh.org itself refuses direct connections (repeated ECONNRESET), but the cited page's indexed content, retrieved via web search, confirms every dated detail: Kalamudia's 1997 public planting of 600 plants in Bilbao with proceedings dismissed; "Kalamudia dissolved in 2001, giving way to local associations that began to cultivate for their members"; Pannagh founded 22 February 2003 and registered in the Basque General Register of Associations 20 June 2003 (No. AS/B/10623/2003); "In 2005, three members of the Bilbao CSC Pannagh were arrested while harvesting... One of the arrestees was Martín Barriuso, president both of Pannagh and of the Spanish Federation of Cannabis Associations (FAC)"; "In 2006... the regional court ruled in favor of Barriuso and his fellow defendants" with previously confiscated cannabis returned to the club for the first time. Corroborated by TNI/Dinafem histories (Dinafem: case "ultimately thrown out, and the 17 kg of crops confiscated were returned"). One secondary source (Dinafem) says four members were arrested rather than three, but the cited source supports the claim as stated.

verdicts.claim: Transform Drug Policy Foundation briefing defines the model (non-profit, closed-membership, collective cultivation), dates the first CSC to 2001, counts roughly 400 clubs, argues Spain proves 'legalisation without commercialisation', with Uruguay and Malta later writing CSCs into statute.
verdicts.evidence: Source confirms verbatim: "Cannabis social clubs (CSCs) are private, non-profit organisations in which cannabis is collectively grown and distributed to registered members."; "The first CSC was founded in 2001..."; "there are thought to be roughly 400 CSCs or similar associations in Spain, most of which are located in Catalonia and the Basque Country"; thesis stated as "The growth of the CSC model in Spain demonstrates that cannabis legalisation does not have to mean commercialisation."; and "Uruguay has made CSCs a key component of its national, legally regulated cannabis market." Malta is not mentioned anywhere in the article.
verdicts.correction: Everything is supported except Malta: the Transform piece names only Uruguay. If the museum text keeps Malta (which did legislate cannabis associations in 2021, after this briefing), it needs a separate citation — it cannot be attributed to this source.

verdicts.claim: Barcelona boom: Catalonia went from ~40 clubs in 2011 to 500+ with 165,000+ members by 2014, at which point city hall ordered closure of a third of the city's 145 clubs and began zoning them; press dubbed Barcelona 'the Amsterdam of southern Europe' (Reason, 2016).
verdicts.evidence: Reason confirms verbatim: "In 2011, just 40 such cannabis clubs existed in Catalonia. By 2014, according to Tio, that number had jumped to more than 500 with over 165,000 members" (Albert Tio, president of AIRAM/FEDCAC), and the nickname "the Amsterdam of southern Europe". But the article never mentions 145 clubs or a closure order for a third of them. What it says: "Recently, more than 50 clubs closed when former Barcelona Mayor Xavier Trias... promised to push through zoning restrictions requiring all clubs within 150 meters of schools, libraries, hospitals, and gyms to close, which would have shut down 80 percent of existing facilities" — and that new mayor Ada Colau "reversed the zoning restrictions" before they took effect.
verdicts.correction: Keep the 40→500+/165,000 figures (attributed to Albert Tio, a club-federation president — an advocate's count, worth flagging) and the nickname. Replace the 'closure of a third of the city's 145 clubs' sentence: this source instead reports 50+ clubs closing under Mayor Trias's threatened 150-meter zoning plan (which would have shut ~80% of clubs) and its reversal by Mayor Colau before implementation. The 46-of-145 closure order of 2014 is reported elsewhere (e.g., Spanish press), not in the cited Reason article — recite it or re-source it.
